penalties_applied.name: requires_human_fulfillment
penalties_applied.reason: Meaningful GCP escalation — writing tickets, navigating vendor support trees, making phone calls, researching zone availability workarounds — requires per-customer human judgment and action that Claude cannot fully automate.

penalties_applied.name: requires_synchronous_human
penalties_applied.reason: Incident response inherently involves time-sensitive coordination: the operator must review the situation, decide on escalation paths, and communicate with the affected team in real time.

rationale: The pain is severe and real — production VM failures with no support recourse is a genuine crisis for paying GCP customers — but the proposed service (escalation brokering, incident monitoring) cannot be delivered autonomously. Each customer incident requires a human to read context, judge severity, contact Google, and coordinate a response; Claude can draft messages but cannot substitute for the actual escalation work. After penalties for per-customer fulfillment and synchronous human involvement, the total drops to 2.9, well below the validate threshold. This is closer to a consulting retainer than an autonomous micro-service.
solution_plan: This idea is not viable as a solo non-technical operator's autonomous micro-service. The core value — actually getting Google to respond and resolving a live production incident — requires a human advocate with GCP expertise making calls and writing escalations. Claude can draft support tickets and synthesize documentation, but the service cannot deliver meaningful results without hands-on human work per customer. A passive monitoring dashboard (alerting when GCP status page changes) is buildable but doesn't solve the core pain of getting support responses. Recommend dropping this opportunity unless reframed as a purely informational product (e.g. a GCP zone availability status aggregator) — but that version has low willingness-to-pay.
notes: Total after penalties is 2.9 — below min_total_to_validate (5.5). The service model is fundamentally consulting-shaped, not product-shaped.
